Precision under pressure

Three CAE-style task types. Select answers and use the explanation buttons whenever an answer needs unpacking.

Part 1 · Multiple-choice cloze

Small actions, big systems

Choose A, B, C or D for each gap.

1. Local repair schemes can ___ a substantial reduction in waste.
2. No single factor can ___ the sudden shift in public attitudes.
3. The decision seemed expensive initially but proved sensible ___.
4. We often ___ reliable public transport until it disappears.
5. The campaign aims to ___ attention to overlooked neighbourhoods.
6. It took residents time to ___ the scale of the disruption.
7. It is worth ___ that the figures are only estimates.
8. Efficiency must not be achieved ___ safety.
Part 2 · Open cloze

The quiet case for boredom

Write one word in each gap, then check your answers.

In a culture that prizes constant activity, boredom is often treated a problem to be eliminated. Yet periods in nothing demands our attention may allow ideas to develop. Researchers have found that people who are left their own devices sometimes make more imaginative connections those given a highly structured task.

This does not mean that every idle moment leads creativity. The point is simply a little mental space can be valuable. It gives the mind an opportunity to wander, rather react. In other words, boredom may be less of a failure more of a resource.

1 treated as; 2 relative pronoun in which; 3 fixed phrase left to one's own devices; 4 comparative more… than; 5 lead to; 6 the point is that; 7 rather than; 8 correlative pair less… and more….

Language focus

Passive forms & passive infinitives

Use the passive to focus on the action or recipient; use reporting structures to distance the speaker from the claim.

Passive: subject + be (correct tense) + past participle  ·  Passive infinitive: be / to be + past participle  ·  Reporting: subject + is/was believed/said/expected + to infinitive / to have + past participle
Time/formPassive formulaExample
Present simpleam/is/are + V3Applications are reviewed weekly.
Past simplewas/were + V3The proposal was rejected.
Present perfecthas/have been + V3A solution has been found.
Past perfecthad been + V3The data had been erased.
Futurewill be + V3The results will be announced.
Modalmodal + be + V3Every claim must be checked.

Reading

Reading between the lines

Activate key vocabulary, rebuild the missing logic of a text, then use its language in a discussion.

Pre-reading

Match word to definition

1. resilient
2. underlying
3. mitigate
4. driving force

Reading Part · Gapped text

What makes a city resilient?

Read the text. Choose the missing paragraph A–F for gaps 1–5. One paragraph is extra.

A This is why local knowledge matters.   B Yet resilience is not simply a matter of rebuilding.   C The result can be a more adaptable city.   D That assumption has been challenged.   E Funding, however, remains uneven.   F It is a lesson that planners increasingly accept.

More than bricks and roads

After a severe flood, a city’s recovery is often measured in visible signs: roads reopened, homes repaired and services restored. It also depends on whether residents can maintain networks, share information and influence decisions.

For decades, experts assumed that technical solutions would automatically protect communities. Engineers now work alongside social researchers to identify the underlying pressures that make some groups particularly vulnerable.

Residents may know which streets become impassable first or which neighbours need extra support. When their experience is ignored, even well-funded projects can fail to meet real needs.

Involving communities early can mitigate risk and build trust.

Post-reading discussion

Use the new vocabulary

  1. Which features make your town or city resilient in a crisis?
  2. What underlying problems should local leaders address before an emergency occurs?
  3. How could a community mitigate the effects of extreme weather?
  4. Who should be the driving force behind change: residents, businesses or government?

Speaking

Think aloud, interact naturally

Four stages of C1 Advanced Speaking, with planning support and a one-minute visual comparison.

Part 1 · Interview

Short personal questions

  • What kind of project would you volunteer for, and why?
  • How has the way you learn changed in recent years?
  • Do you prefer solving practical problems alone or collaboratively?
Useful start: “I’d say that…”, “What appeals to me most is…”, “It depends largely on…”
Part 2 · Long turn

Compare and speculate — 1 minute

Compare the photos and answer: Why might people choose to take part in these activities, and which activity is more likely to have a long-term impact?

Compare: “Both photos show…”, “Whereas…”, “They may be motivated by…”, “This could have a greater impact because…”
Part 3 · Collaborative task

Spidergram: a better local initiative

With a partner, discuss which two ideas would most improve community wellbeing. Reach a decision.

community wellbeing

Ideas: repair café · mentoring scheme · public garden · skills exchange · quiet study hub

Part 4 · Discussion

Go beyond the task

  • Should governments encourage volunteering, or should it remain entirely voluntary?
  • Can small local initiatives genuinely influence national problems?
  • How might technology strengthen — or weaken — a sense of community?
  • What makes people sustain a commitment after initial enthusiasm fades?
Extend: “That raises the question of…”, “I take your point; however…”, “A possible consequence is…”
06

Writing Part 1

Build a persuasive CAE essay

A strong essay answers every note, develops a clear position and uses an appropriate academic register.

Four-paragraph blueprint

  1. Introduction: reframe the issue and state your position.
  2. Body 1: develop the first required point with reason/example.
  3. Body 2: develop the second required point and another perspective.
  4. Conclusion: weigh the arguments and give a justified final view.

Target: 220–260 words. Cover all three notes; do not use headings or informal contractions.

Language bank

Introduce: It is often argued that… / There is little doubt that…
Develop: A compelling argument is that… / This is particularly relevant when…
Balance: Granted, …; nevertheless, … / While this may be true, …
Conclude: On balance, … / The most convincing case is therefore…
Your CAE essay task

“Local authorities should spend more money on public spaces than on online services.” Do you agree?

Write about: 1) access for different groups, 2) community life, 3) your own idea.

Write 220–260 words. Use all notes and give reasons for your point of view.
